source: Kurvers et al. (2016) Boosting medical diagnostics by pooling independent judgments
finding: Majority or confidence-weighted pooling of independent doctors beat the best single doctor only when the doctors had similar accuracy. When accuracy differed a lot, the best doctor won.
numbers: Over 140 doctors, over 20,000 diagnoses (mammography and skin cancer). Pooling beat the best member only when the accuracy gap |dJ| < 0.1; holds for groups of 2, 3, 5. Pooling always beat the average member.
limits: Simulation on real data, not live groups. Binary diagnoses. Independent judgments assumed.
agent_relevance: Condorcet gain needs similar competence as well as independence. In S7, voting over one strong generator and weak ones can lose to the strong one alone. Check the competence gap before pooling.

source: Lorenz, Rauhut, Schweitzer, Helbing (2011) How social influence can undermine the wisdom of crowd effect
finding: Showing people others' estimates shrank diversity without reducing collective error. The truth moved to the edge of the estimate range and confidence rose.
numbers: N=144, 5 estimation rounds, control vs average-info vs full-info. Arithmetic mean closer to truth than individuals in only 21.3% of cases; geometric mean on logs in 77.1%.
quote: social influence diminishes the diversity of the crowd without improvements of its collective error
limits: Right-skewed estimation questions; small lab groups; contradicted for decentralized networks (see Becker 2017).
agent_relevance: Letting voters see each other's answers breaks independence (G4). Keep samples blind to each other until the code step.

source: Becker, Brackbill, Centola (2017) Network dynamics of social influence in the wisdom of crowds
finding: Replicated the diversity loss of Lorenz but showed accuracy rose in decentralized networks. In centralized networks, a biased hub made groups worse.
numbers: 13 decentralized trials: SD of estimates fell 43% (round 1 to 3); median error fell from 0.76 SD to 0.67 SD (12%); mean error 0.69 to 0.62 (10%); average individual error fell 23%. 1,040 subjects, 4,340 estimates.
limits: Revision size correlated with initial error (rho 0.41), so wrong people moved more. Outcome depends on network structure and on whether the hub is near truth.
agent_relevance: Partial failed replication of the claim that any influence hurts. Interaction can help if errors get corrected, which the LLM debate studies below test.

source: Satopaa, Pemantle, Ungar (2015) Modeling probability forecasts via information diversity
finding: Optimal extremizing of an averaged probability depends on how much information forecasters share. Less overlap means more extremizing is right. Gives a principled reason for a practice that was ad hoc.
numbers: On 44 GJP superforecasters, 123 events (23 occurred), 17-34 forecasts per event: mean Brier 0.132 (plain average), 0.128 (log-odds), 0.128 (probit), 0.123 (their model). Uncertainty term 0.152.
limits: Gain is about 0.009 Brier over plain averaging on one elite group. Needs a model of overlap.
agent_relevance: G4 forbids extremizing LLM votes. This paper says why: extremizing is right only for forecasters with distinct information, which samples of one model lack.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd: LLM ensemble prediction, Study 1
finding: Median of 12 LLMs matched a human crowd on 31 binary questions. Individual models were mostly worse than the crowd. Models showed acquiescence: mean forecasts above 50% though outcomes were near even.
numbers: 12 LLMs vs 925 humans. LLM crowd mean Brier 0.20 (SD 0.12) vs human 0.19 (SD 0.19), t(60)=0.19, p=0.85. Equivalence at d=0.5 bounds (0.081 Brier). Single models: GPT-4 0.15 best, Coral 0.38 worst.
limits: Only 31 questions. Equivalence bounds wide. No direct independence test.
agent_relevance: A median across different model families is a baseline S7 aggregator for probabilities. Pooling does not remove acquiescence bias.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd, Study 2: human median as information
finding: Showing the human crowd median to an LLM improved its Brier score, but simply averaging human and machine forecasts did better than letting the LLM update.
numbers: GPT-4 Brier 0.17 to 0.14 (p=0.003); Claude 2 0.22 to 0.15 (p<0.001). 186 forecasts each. Update size correlated with distance to human median (r=0.88 GPT-4, 0.87 Claude 2). Abstract: gains 17-28%.
limits: Same 31 questions. Anchoring on the crowd gives less than a simple average.
agent_relevance: Do the averaging in code (G5) rather than asking the model to update toward a stated answer.

source: Schoenegger, Park, Karger, Trott, Tetlock (2024) AI-augmented predictions: LLM assistants improve human forecasting accuracy
finding: Humans who used an LLM assistant forecast better, even with a deliberately noisy overconfident assistant. Data did not consistently show loss of crowd diversity.
numbers: N=991, six questions. Accuracy up 24-28% vs control (preregistered). Without one outlier item: 41% (superforecasting assistant) vs 29% (noisy assistant).
limits: Outlier-driven; diversity-loss hypothesis tested but not consistently supported; short task.
agent_relevance: A shared helper may homogenize answers in theory, but this study did not show it. Weak evidence either way.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: A retrieval LLM system with trimmed-mean ensembling came near the crowd but did not beat it overall. Trimmed mean was best of five aggregators on validation.
numbers: Test Brier 0.179 vs crowd 0.149 (random 0.250); accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%. Best baseline model 0.208. Aggregators tried: mean, median, geometric mean, trimmed mean, universal self-consistency.
limits: Gap of 0.03 Brier. System beat the crowd only in a selective setting. Standard calibration fixes did not help.
agent_relevance: A trimmed mean of sampled forecasts is a safe code-side aggregator; extremizing was not needed because output was already calibrated.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities
finding: Superforecasters beat the general public and every LLM. The best LLMs were behind, and the best ones used the crowd forecast as input.
numbers: Brier: superforecasters 0.096 vs public 0.121 (p<0.001) vs best LLM (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) 0.122 on the 200-item subset. Second table: superforecasters 0.076, public 0.096, GPT-4o 0.130. The 0.054 gap is about twice the GPT-4 to GPT-4o gap (0.026). A 3-model x 3-prompt ensemble baseline was built with median, geometric mean and log-odds geometric mean.
limits: Ensemble row not read in detail. Benchmark moves over time.
agent_relevance: Pooling LLMs had not closed the gap to expert humans on dynamic questions by 2025; do not assume votes equal expertise.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning
finding: Sampling many reasoning paths and taking the most common answer beat greedy chain of thought.
numbers: Gains: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-challenge +3.9 points.
limits: Gains shrink on easier or knowledge tasks. Samples come from one model, so errors are correlated.
agent_relevance: Founding LLM case of Condorcet-style voting. The gain is real but bounded by shared errors (G4).

source: Li et al. (2024) More agents is all you need (Agent Forest)
finding: Sampling and voting scales with the number of agents; the gain grows with task difficulty. A small model with enough votes passes a larger single model.
numbers: GSM8K: Llama2-13B with ensemble 59% vs Llama2-70B single 54%. Gains 4-9% on HumanEval. 10 independent runs; ensemble sizes 1-40.
limits: Gains flatten with size. Orthogonal to other methods, but still one model family.
agent_relevance: Voting size has diminishing returns; budget accordingly.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Are more LM calls all you need? Scaling properties of compound AI systems
finding: Majority-vote accuracy can rise then fall with more calls, because on hard queries the wrong answer is the mode and more votes lock it in. Condorcet's competence condition fails per query.
numbers: Example hard query: correct answer 34% vs wrong answer 56%; easy query: correct 67%. On MMLU Physics, 53% of queries easy, 47% hard (Vote). Predicted optimal number of calls matched the observed optimum on the tested datasets (MMLU Physics, TruthfulQA, GPQA, AVeriTeC).
quote: more LM calls lead to higher performance on easy queries, but lower performance on hard queries
limits: Few-option answers; assumes independent calls from a fixed model.
agent_relevance: Per-query competence is what matters. Vote breaks on hard items. Treat agreement as a hint and escalate to checks (G3) when the top answer share is low.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large language monkeys: scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
finding: Coverage (some sample is right) keeps rising with samples, but majority vote and reward models plateau.
numbers: MATH, Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000. Majority vote or reward-model selection only 40.50% to 41.41%. SWE-bench Lite: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250 (verifier available), above the 43% single-sample state of the art.
limits: The gap matters where no automatic verifier exists. Voting plateaus near 100 samples.
agent_relevance: Main support for G3 and G5: with a verifier, many samples pay; without one, votes saturate.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Mixture-of-Agents enhances large language model capabilities
finding: Layering several different LLMs as proposers and aggregators topped AlpacaEval 2.0 with open models.
numbers: AlpacaEval 2.0 LC win rate 65.1% vs 57.5% for GPT-4 Omni.
limits: The aggregator is an LLM, so model-judge biases apply. Li 2025 disputes the benefit of mixing.
agent_relevance: Aggregation by a model sees all drafts; our G5 prefers code selection.

source: Li, Lin, Xia, Jin (2025) Rethinking mixture-of-agents: is mixing different LLMs beneficial?
finding: Repeating the single best model (Self-MoA) beat mixing different models in most settings, because mixing lowers average quality. Mixing helps only when models are each strong on different subtasks.
numbers: Self-MoA +6.6 points on AlpacaEval 2.0 over Mixed-MoA; +3.8 average across MMLU, CRUX, MATH. 200+ experiments; MoA performance correlated positively with both quality and diversity (Vendi score) with a Pareto trade-off; best at high quality and relatively low diversity.
limits: Challenge to model-diversity claims. Tasks where one model dominates.
agent_relevance: Condorcet needs competence above chance for each voter. Weak voters can hurt; prefer the strongest model with varied samples unless a weaker model is complementary.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop overvaluing multi-agent debate
finding: Five debate methods on 9 benchmarks with 4 models often failed to beat single-agent chain of thought or self-consistency, despite more compute. Mixing two different models helped debate consistently.
numbers: Heter-SoM +6.4% and Heter-EoT +8.2% over same-model averages (9 benchmarks); vs CoT-average +2.1 to +5.8%. On MMLU with Claude-3.5-haiku only one debate framework beat CoT (+0.85%); the others were at least 3.60% worse.
limits: Gains vary by dataset; some negative (e.g. -10.8% on MBPP in one row).
agent_relevance: Debate is not a free boost. Model heterogeneity beats extra rounds of talk.

source: Choi, Zhu, Li (2025) Debate or vote: which yields better decisions in multi-agent LLMs?
finding: Majority voting alone accounts for most of the gain attributed to debate. Theory: debate makes each agent's belief a martingale, so expected correctness does not improve from talk alone.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, 7 benchmarks, average accuracy: single agent 0.7205; decentralized debate (T=2) 0.7377, (T=5) 0.7050; centralized debate (T=2) 0.6551; majority voting 0.7691. An oracle-biased belief update raised MMLU formal logic from 0.5000 to 0.6825.
limits: Single model family in the table read; oracle variant is not deployable.
agent_relevance: Strong support for voting in code over debate; debate helps only if updates are biased toward correction by a real check (G2).

source: Kaesberg et al. (2025) Voting or consensus? Decision-making in multi-agent debate
finding: Seven decision rules compared with all else fixed. Voting rules helped reasoning tasks; consensus rules helped knowledge tasks. More agents helped; more discussion rounds before voting hurt.
numbers: Voting +13.2% on reasoning tasks; consensus +2.8% on knowledge tasks; proposed AAD up to +3.3%, CI up to +7.4%.
limits: Gains are relative to other protocols, not to one model; benchmark-specific. Abstract read only.
agent_relevance: The aggregation rule should depend on task type: unanimity suits facts, plurality suits reasoning.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD? A look at multi-agent debate strategies
finding: Multi-agent debate in current form does not reliably beat self-consistency or ensembling with multiple prompts. With tuned hyperparameters some debate systems (Multi-Persona) did better.
numbers: Abstract level read; no per-benchmark numbers recorded.
limits: Result depends on hyperparameters; authors say debate is hard to optimize.
agent_relevance: Ensembling is the fair baseline any debate step must beat.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Rethinking the bounds of LLM reasoning: are multi-agent discussions the key?
finding: A single agent with strong prompts (a demonstration or a detailed question description) nearly matched the best multi-agent discussion framework. Discussion beat a single agent mainly when no demonstration was in the prompt.
numbers: Evaluated on FOLIO-wiki and other reasoning tasks across several backbones (exact accuracies not recorded).
limits: Numbers not extracted from tables; abstract and figure caption read.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation for debate gains: they replace missing prompt quality.

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving factuality and reasoning through multiagent debate
finding: Debate among instances raised factual accuracy over a single agent and over self-reflection.
numbers: Biographies 66.0 single, 68.3 reflection, 73.8 debate; MMLU 63.9, 57.7, 71.1; chess move validity 29.3, 38.8, 45.2. Different personas on MMLU lifted 71.1 to 74.2.
limits: Later work (Choi 2025, Zhang 2025) finds voting explains most of the gain.
agent_relevance: The positive result that others failed to isolate; treat as an upper bound.

source: Verga et al. (2024) Replacing judges with juries: a panel of diverse models (PoLL)
finding: A panel of three smaller judges from different families agreed better with humans than one GPT-4 judge, with less intra-model bias and about 7x lower cost.
numbers: Cohen's kappa vs human on NQ / TriviaQA / HotpotQA: PoLL 0.763 / 0.906 / 0.867; GPT-4 0.627 / 0.841 / 0.830. Max-vote pooling on QA.
limits: Judging tasks with reference answers; pool of 3.
agent_relevance: Pooling judges from different families supports the G4 diversity logic for any judge step.

source: Kim, Garg, Peng, Garg (2025) Correlated errors in large language models
finding: LLM errors are highly correlated: models agree about 60% of the time when both are wrong, vs 33% by chance. More accurate models are more correlated, even across providers.
numbers: 349 LLMs on 12,032 questions (HuggingFace), 71 on 14,042 (HELM), 20 on 1,800 resumes. Mean wrong-wrong agreement 0.423 (HF) and 0.6 (HELM). Some pairs near 0.97-0.9987. Features explain 34-62% of variance. Judges inflate the accuracy of weaker models.
limits: Mostly multiple choice; correlation measured on errors only.
agent_relevance: Direct test of Condorcet independence for LLM ensembles: it fails, and gets worse as models improve. Pick voters from distinct providers and expect limited gain.

source: Lefort et al. (2024) Examining independence in ensemble sentiment analysis using the Condorcet Jury Theorem
finding: Majority vote across fine-tuned GPT-3.5, DistilRoBERTa and FinBERT added almost nothing. Authors infer the independence condition fails.
numbers: Fine-tuned precision/recall about 0.49-0.51 / 0.53-0.54 (random 0.33). Ensemble vs best single (SFT GPT-3.5): differences 0.00 to 0.01 on precision and recall, -0.01 on another metric.
limits: Three-class financial sentiment; errors spread uniformly over wrong labels; the independence conclusion is inferred, not directly tested.
agent_relevance: Simple empirical Condorcet test: if bagging adds zero, voters are not independent.

source: List (2005) The probability of inconsistencies in complex collective decisions
finding: The doctrinal paradox is likely under plausible conditions. Premise-wise majority voting yields an inconsistent collective set with a probability that tends to 1 or 0 depending on voter competence and premise truth.
numbers: 3 voters: 0.0938 under impartial culture; limit 0.25 as n grows. With pTT=0.3, pTF=pFT=0.25, pFF=0.2: n=11 0.3211, n=101 0.7113, n=1501 0.9999. Premises true and competence low (but above chance): limit 1; high competence: limit 0.
limits: Model assumes independence and a specific rule R iff (P and Q); theoretical.
agent_relevance: Premise-wise majorities can contradict the conclusion. In code, check consistency of the combined answer set (G3) and pick premise-based or conclusion-based rule explicitly.

source: Genest & Zidek (1986) Combining probability distributions: a critique and annotated bibliography
finding: Review of linear and logarithmic pools. The linear pool does not preserve independence or external Bayesianity; the log pool is externally Bayesian. No single pool meets all desirable axioms.
numbers: Not opened (page blocked); from background knowledge.
limits: Unopened; verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Choose a pool by the property needed: log pool for updating consistency, linear for robustness.

source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem (surprisingly popular)
finding: Choosing the answer that is more popular than people predicted beat majority vote when the crowd is mostly wrong.
numbers: From memory, not verified: error cut about 21.3% vs majority vote and about 24.2% vs confidence-weighted across four studies. Paywalled; recheck.
limits: Needs respondents' predictions of others' answers; unopened.
agent_relevance: Candidate aggregator when the majority is suspect; needs a second elicitation question.

source: Hong & Page (2004) Groups of diverse problem solvers can outperform groups of high-ability problem solvers
finding: Claimed diversity can beat ability in problem-solving groups. Later critiques (Thompson 2014) say the result depends on restrictive assumptions.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Contested; background only.
agent_relevance: Cautions against assuming diversity beats quality; consistent with Self-MoA.

source: Mellers et al. (2014, 2015) Superforecaster studies (Good Judgment Project)
finding: Training, teaming and tracking raised accuracy; top forecasters stayed good. Aggregation with extremizing beat the plain mean.
numbers: Not opened; effect sizes not verified (Satopaa 2015 above uses GJP superforecaster data).
limits: Unopened.
agent_relevance: Supports calibration-training analogies; do not copy numbers.
